title: Ibn al-Nafis and the Heart
summary: How the thirteenth-century physician Ibn al-Nafis challenged an old idea about the heart and was the first to describe how blood travels from the heart to the lungs and back.
poll: A scientist should question an idea even when famous experts believe it.

versions.title: The Man Who Knew the Heart
versions.text:
Put your hand on your chest. Do you feel a beat? That is your heart. It is a pump. It pumps blood all day. It pumps all night, too.

Long ago, a man named Ibn al-Nafis lived. He was born in Damascus. That was long, long ago. He was a doctor. He went to work in Cairo. He ran a big hospital there.

In his time, most doctors had an old idea. There is a wall in the heart. They said blood went through holes in the wall. That is how it got from side to side.

Ibn al-Nafis said no. The wall is thick. It has no holes. He said blood goes from the heart to the lungs. In the lungs, it mixes with air. Then it goes back to the heart.

He was right! But his books were lost for a long time. In 1924, a doctor found one. Now we know he was first.

versions.title: The Man Who Knew the Heart
versions.text:
Put your hand on your chest. Can you feel a beat? That is your heart. It is a strong pump. It pumps blood all day and all night.

Long ago, a man named Ibn al-Nafis lived. He was born in Damascus in about 1213. He became a doctor. Later he moved to Cairo. There he led a big hospital.

In his time, most doctors had an old idea about the heart. They thought blood went from one side of the heart to the other side. They said it went through tiny holes in a wall in the middle.

Ibn al-Nafis did not agree. He said the wall is thick. It has no holes. So blood must take a new path. It goes from the heart to the lungs. In the lungs, it mixes with air. Then it goes back to the heart.

He was right! But for hundreds of years, his books were lost. In 1924, a doctor found one of them. Now we know that Ibn al-Nafis found this path first.

About 800 years ago, a man named Ibn al-Nafis was born in Damascus. He studied hard and became a doctor. Later he moved to Cairo, in Egypt. There he led a large hospital and wrote many books.

At that time, most doctors believed an old idea about the heart. They thought blood passed from one side of the heart to the other side through tiny holes in the wall in the middle.

Ibn al-Nafis did not agree. He said the wall is thick and has no holes. So blood must travel a different way. He said blood leaves the right side of the heart and goes to the lungs. In the lungs, it mixes with air. Then it flows back to the left side of the heart.

He was right! But his books were forgotten for hundreds of years. In 1924, an Egyptian doctor found one of his books in a library. Today, Ibn al-Nafis is known as the first to explain this path.

versions.title: Ibn al-Nafis and the Heart
versions.text:
Put your hand on your chest. Can you feel a steady beat? That is your heart at work. Your heart is a strong pump that pushes blood around your whole body, day and night.

About 800 years ago, a boy named Ibn al-Nafis was born in Damascus. He studied medicine at a famous hospital there and became a doctor. Later he moved to Cairo, in Egypt. There he led a large hospital, taught students, and wrote many books.

At that time, most doctors followed an old idea from a Greek doctor named Galen. Galen said that blood passed from the right side of the heart to the left side through tiny holes in the wall between them.

Ibn al-Nafis did not agree. He said the wall is thick and has no holes at all. So blood must travel a different way. He wrote that blood leaves the right side of the heart and goes to the lungs. In the lungs, it mixes with air. Then it flows back to the left side of the heart, which pumps it to the body.

He was right! But his books were forgotten for hundreds of years. In 1924, an Egyptian doctor found one of them in a library in Germany. Today, Ibn al-Nafis is known as the first to describe this path.

versions.title: Ibn al-Nafis and the Heart
versions.text:
Place your hand on your chest, and you will feel a steady beat. That is your heart. It is a strong pump that pushes blood around your body every second of the day.

Your heart has four parts called chambers. Two are on the right side, and two are on the left side. A thick wall of muscle runs down the middle.

About 800 years ago, Ibn al-Nafis was born in Damascus. He studied medicine at a famous hospital there and became a skilled physician. Later he moved to Cairo. There he led a large hospital, taught students, and wrote many books.

At that time, most doctors followed a theory from Galen, a Greek doctor who had lived about a thousand years earlier. Galen taught that blood passed from the right chamber of the heart to the left chamber through tiny holes in the wall.

Ibn al-Nafis disagreed. He wrote that the wall is thick and has no holes. Instead, blood must leave the right side of the heart and travel to the lungs. There it mixes with air and picks up what we now call oxygen. Then it returns to the left side of the heart, which pumps it out to the body. This path is part of the circulation of blood.

When he died in 1288, he left his house and his library to a hospital in Cairo. He wanted others to keep learning.

His discovery was right, but it was forgotten for centuries. About 300 years later, doctors in Europe described the same path. Then, in 1924, an Egyptian doctor found a manuscript by Ibn al-Nafis in a library in Berlin. It proved that he had explained this path first.

versions.title: Ibn al-Nafis and the Pulmonary Circulation
versions.text:
Place your hand on your chest, and you will feel a steady beat. That is your heart, a muscular pump that pushes blood throughout your body every second of the day, and understanding exactly how it works took doctors many centuries.

The heart is divided into four chambers. The two upper chambers receive blood, while the two lower chambers, called ventricles, pump it out, and a thick wall of muscle known as the septum separates the right side from the left side.

Ibn al-Nafis was born in Damascus around 1213, and he studied medicine at a famous hospital there before moving to Cairo. In Cairo he became the head of a large hospital, taught many students, and wrote numerous books, including a commentary on the anatomy section of a famous medical encyclopedia by Ibn Sina.

At that time, most doctors accepted a theory from Galen, a Greek physician who had lived about a thousand years earlier. Galen taught that blood passed from the right ventricle to the left ventricle through tiny invisible pores in the septum.

In his commentary, Ibn al-Nafis rejected this idea. He wrote that the septum is solid and has no pores, so blood must leave the right ventricle and travel to the lungs. There it mixes with air, picking up what we now call oxygen, and then returns to the left side of the heart, which pumps it out to the rest of the body. This loop between the heart and lungs is now known as the pulmonary circulation.

When he died in 1288, Ibn al-Nafis left his house and his library to a hospital in Cairo, so that future doctors could keep learning from his work.

Unfortunately, his discovery remained unknown in Europe. About three hundred years later, European scientists described the same loop, and in 1628 the English doctor William Harvey explained how blood circulates through the entire body. Then, in 1924, an Egyptian doctor found Ibn al-Nafis's manuscript in a library in Berlin, which proved that he had described the pulmonary circulation first.

versions.title: Ibn al-Nafis and the Pulmonary Circulation
versions.text:
Place your hand on your chest, and you will feel a steady, rhythmic beat. That is your heart, a powerful muscular pump that propels blood throughout your body every second of the day, and understanding precisely how it functions occupied physicians for many centuries.

The heart is divided into four chambers: the two upper chambers receive incoming blood, while the two lower chambers, called ventricles, pump it outward, and a thick muscular partition known as the septum separates the right side from the left side.

Ibn al-Nafis was born in Damascus around 1213, and he studied medicine at a renowned hospital there before relocating to Cairo. In Cairo he became the director of a prominent hospital, educated numerous students, and composed many books, including an extensive commentary on the anatomy section of an influential medical encyclopedia by Ibn Sina called The Canon of Medicine.

At that time, most physicians accepted a theory from Galen, a Greek doctor who had lived approximately a thousand years earlier, who taught that blood passed from the right ventricle to the left ventricle through tiny invisible pores in the septum.

In his commentary, Ibn al-Nafis rejected this explanation, arguing that the septum is solid and contains no pores, so blood must exit the right ventricle and travel to the lungs. There it mixes with air, absorbing what we now call oxygen, and subsequently returns to the left side of the heart, which pumps it to the remainder of the body. This circuit between the heart and lungs is now known as the pulmonary circulation.

When he died in 1288, Ibn al-Nafis donated his house and his library to a hospital in Cairo, ensuring that subsequent generations of physicians could continue benefiting from his scholarship.

Unfortunately, his discovery remained unknown in Europe for centuries. Approximately three hundred years later, European anatomists described the identical circuit, and in 1628 the English physician William Harvey explained how blood circulates throughout the entire body. Then, in 1924, an Egyptian physician discovered Ibn al-Nafis's manuscript in a library in Berlin, which demonstrated conclusively that he had described the pulmonary circulation first. Today, historians of medicine regard him as one of the most remarkable and original physicians of the medieval world, whose careful reasoning about anatomy challenged an authority that had gone unquestioned for a thousand years.

wrong.C: He worked in a hospital, but the article is not about building hospitals.

questions.stem: Why did Ibn al-Nafis think blood must go to the lungs?
options: He saw it in a dream.
The wall in the heart is thick and has no holes.
His teacher told him so.
The lungs are much, much bigger than the heart is.

wrong.A: The article says nothing about a dream.
wrong.C: He disagreed with what most doctors taught.
wrong.D: The size of the lungs is not his reason.

It pushes blood around the body.

wrong.B: The stomach holds food, not the heart.

wrong.D: Holes are part of the old wrong idea about the heart wall.

He was not afraid to say an old idea was wrong.
He did not like working in big hospitals at all.
He wanted his books to be lost.

wrong.A: He wrote books, so he must have read and studied.
wrong.D: Nothing says he wanted his books lost.

HIGH.prompt: Explain how Ibn al-Nafis used evidence about the septum to challenge Galen, and why his discovery was not recognized until 1924.
checklist: I explained Galen's theory and why Ibn al-Nafis rejected it.
I described the pulmonary circulation using the words ventricle and septum.
I explained why his work was forgotten and how it was rediscovered.
HIGH.modelAnswer: Ibn al-Nafis used evidence about the septum, the thick wall of muscle between the heart's two sides, to challenge Galen's ancient theory that blood passed through invisible holes in that wall. He argued that because the septum has no such holes, blood must instead travel from the right ventricle to the lungs, where it absorbs oxygen, before returning to the left side of the heart in what we now call pulmonary circulation. Although his explanation was correct, it was not recognized for centuries because few people read his manuscript, and only in 1924 did an Egyptian doctor discover it in a library in Berlin, finally proving that Ibn al-Nafis had described this path long before European doctors did.
